topic: A USB-C cable's watts and its data speed are two different numbers

experiment.change: first reel built for the SHOT VARIETY check (24 Nov): seven different objects or views (plug macro, laptop and drive wide, sliced cable, two cutaway cables, bars, spec tag), a cut every 3-5 s, each cut a different kind; the cable's two lanes (amber power, cyan data) are the one picture

lines.text: A USB-C cable can charge a laptop at 240 watts.
Plug the same cable into a hard drive, and the data can crawl.
One cable, two lanes: power and data.
Apple's own 240 watt cable sends data at USB 2 rates.
Its Thunderbolt 4 Pro cable moves 40 gigabits a second, and charges up to 100 watts.
So a bigger watt number does not mean faster data.
Before you buy, read both numbers: watts and speed.

post.title: Your USB-C cable has two numbers
post.caption:
A USB-C cable has TWO numbers, and most people only read one 🔌

Watts = how much power it can carry. Speed = how fast it moves data. They are separate.

Apple's own 240W USB-C Charge Cable supports charging of up to 240 watts but transfers data at USB 2 rates. Apple's Thunderbolt 4 Pro Cable supports data up to 40Gb/s and charging up to 100W.

So a bigger watt number does NOT mean faster data. (Same plug, different jobs.)

Before you buy a cable for a laptop, a drive or a phone, read both numbers: watts and speed. If the box only lists one, it is only half the story.

Which do you buy cables for more: charging or transferring files? Charging or files 👇 Send this to the friend who has a drawer full of random cables.
